Days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly adding new evidence in the trade secrets lawsuit. Today, Apple counters that OpenAI went beyond what court rules permit in its response. Here are the details.

Apple claims OpenAI went beyond simply opposing the new evidence.

In Apple's lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products over suspected theft of proprietary information, one piece involves a request for a preliminary injunction.

In short, Apple has asked the court to issue a preliminary injunction, arguing this would prevent its trade secrets from further being incorporated into OpenAI's hardware development during the pendency of the case.

In the legal back-and-forth over that request, Apple submitted an opposition brief with five accompanying expert declarations. Defendants in turn claimed Apple improperly introduced new evidence and asked the court to strike portions of it.

In their opposition, OpenAI and other defendants not only accused Apple of introducing new evidence, but also filed multiple documents to counter Apple's claims.

Apple today filed a reply to that opposition, arguing defendants did not merely oppose the new evidence, but raised new arguments and testimony:

「Rule 7-3(d)(1)」 allows a party to oppose new evidence in an opposition brief, but also states that filing 「shall not be further argued in the motion.」 Defendants did not comply with that limit; instead they used their filing to re-litigate the merits of Apple's preliminary-injunction motion. For example, defendants questioned whether Dr. Runge had 「any basis to offer any analysis,」 whether he adequately responded to 「countervailing evidence,」 and whether he could show certain Apple materials were not publicly available.⋯⋯These arguments are not oppositions to new evidence.⋯⋯(「Statements that some of plaintiff's positions are not supported by or contradicted by other testimony」 are not 「oppositions to evidence.」)

Apple also objected to one of Liu's new declarations, calling it the 「most serious overreach」 in defendants' filing:

Under such circumstances, when defendants submitted Liu's declaration, they argued the court should consider that declaration only if it simultaneously decided to consider the Apple evidence under challenge.

Having said that, Apple argues that because defendants have now raised new arguments on their own, the court should consider the whole record rather than striking anything from Apple's opposition brief:

The court is set to hear Apple's preliminary-injunction motion on October 14.
